The Wild Robot

When a machine programmed to serve learns to be a mother in the wild — DreamWorks tells its kindest story in years.

Director Chris Sanders Year 2024 Runtime 102 min Rated PG Rating 4.5 / 5
DN
Dat Nguyen
Review by Dat Nguyen · Film Review
9.0
ExcellentOut of 10
About a 3-minute read
Genre: Animation · Adventure · Family

Some animated films delight children in the cinema and leave adults quiet on the way home. The Wild Robot belongs to that rare second group. At first glance, it is a familiar fairy tale about a robot lost deep in the forest. But the deeper it goes, the further it moves away from the family-adventure formula, becoming a gentle, lingering reflection on parenthood, on community, and on choosing to live kindly in a world that runs on survival instinct.

01 — The StoryA Machine Learns to Be a Mother

After a storm, service robot ROZZUM 7134 — Roz for short — washes up on an uninhabited island. Programmed to complete any task she is given, Roz eagerly looks for a “customer” among the wild animals, who only want to drive her away. An unexpected accident makes her the reluctant mother of Brightbill, an orphaned gosling who, newly hatched, takes Roz as his only family. With the cunning fox Fink and the experienced opossum Pinktail, Roz takes on a task that sounds simple but is brutally demanding: raise Brightbill until he is big enough, teach him to swim, teach him to fly, before winter arrives and the geese migrate.

02 — The VisualsA Painting in Motion

The first thing that overwhelms the viewer is the imagery. Director Chris Sanders — the filmmaker behind Lilo & Stitch and How to Train Your Dragon — and the DreamWorks team abandon the familiar glossy surface of 3D animation in favour of a hand-painted, oil-painting style. Every frame is a painting: sunlight through the canopy, a lake washed with colour at sunset, a snowstorm swallowing the whole forest in white. Roz begins bright and flawless, like a product on display; over time, her shell is scratched, moss-covered, marked by rain and sun — nature itself is slowly rewriting her.

“Sometimes, to survive, we must become more than we were programmed to be.”

The film’s central line

03 — Voice PerformancesThe Heart Is in the Journey to Motherhood

But technique is only half the story. The heart of the film lies in Roz learning to be a mother — something that was never in her original programming. Lupita Nyong’o voices Roz with a warm, measured tone, letting the initial mechanical quality melt away into worry, confusion, and then unconditional love. Pedro Pascal turns the fox Fink from a con artist into a charming companion, while Kit Connor gives Brightbill the very real stubbornness of a child growing up and beginning to question where he came from. The moment Brightbill learns the truth about the family he lost is one of the quietest and most aching passages in recent animation.

04 — Music & PacingNot Perfect, but Whole

Kris Bowers’ music supports the emotion without overwhelming it, especially in the almost wordless passages near the beginning and in the winter climax at the end. The film is not perfect: the third act moves rather fast, and the villains from the corporation that built Roz arrive a little late and are dealt with more quickly than expected. Even so, the message it leaves behind remains whole: kindness is not a weakness, but a choice to be practised every day — just as the whole forest learns to survive the winter together, instead of each creature fending for itself.

05 — ConclusionThe Editors’ Closing Word

The Wild Robot is proof that family animation can still be heartbreakingly beautiful and tell a story deep enough for adults to see themselves in it. A film to watch with the family — and to sit with in silence for a few minutes after the screen goes dark.

Verdict

One of the most beautiful and humane animated films of 2024. The Wild Robot wins you over with painterly images, subtle voice performances, and a message about kindness strong enough to reach every age.
